# 🛰️ First Satellite vs. Latest Satellite

## 🚀 The First: Sputnik 1 (1957)

Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite, launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on **4 October 1957**.

- **Size & Shape:** It was a polished metal sphere **58 cm (23 in)** in diameter with four external radio antennas to broadcast radio pulses.
- **Weight:** Sputnik 1 weighed **83.6 kg (184 pounds)**.
- **Instruments/Technology:** It was an extremely simple satellite — a metal sphere with four long antennas protruding from it. It contained a thermometer, a fan, a radio transmitter, batteries, and little else.
- **Purpose:** The only cargo on board was a low-power radio transmitter, which broadcast a beeping noise at regular intervals — a signal that could be heard by radio listeners around the world.
- **Orbit:** Sputnik 1's orbit was elliptical — approximately 230 km from Earth at its closest point (perigee) and 940 km away at its furthest point (apogee). It took just under an hour and a half to circle the entire planet.
- **Lifespan:** It sent a radio signal back to Earth for three weeks before its three silver-zinc batteries became depleted. Aerodynamic drag caused it to fall back into the atmosphere on 4 January 1958.
- **Historical Impact:** The satellite's success was unanticipated by the United States, which precipitated the "Sputnik crisis" and triggered the start of the Space Race.

---

## 🌐 One of the Latest: ViaSat-3 F3 (2026)

ViaSat-3 Flight 3 (VS-3 F3) successfully launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a **SpaceX Falcon Heavy** rocket on **April 29, 2026**.

- **Type:** The VS-3 constellation is comprised of three **Ka-band satellites**, each designed to be capable of rapidly shifting capacity throughout its coverage area to deliver bandwidth where and when it's needed most.
- **Orbit:** Launching on a Falcon Heavy rocket reduces time to orbit by delivering the satellite to a more favorable transfer orbit, where the satellite's electric propulsion takes over to place ViaSat-3 F3 in **geostationary orbit**. Following launch, the satellite will spend several months traveling to geostationary orbit.
- **Capacity:** ViaSat-3 F3 is designed to expand Viasat's global network with **more than 1 Tbps (terabit per second)** of throughput over the Asia-Pacific region.
- **Technology:** The ViaSat-3 satellites are designed with state-of-the-art technology to maximize efficient, flexible bandwidth deployment and provide enhanced performance for commercial mobility, fixed services, and defense customers.
- **Purpose/Coverage:** ViaSat-3 F3 is the final satellite in the ViaSat-3 constellation and is designed to deliver regional coverage across the **Asia-Pacific (APAC) region**.
- **Advanced Capabilities:** Viasat believes the VS-3 satellites are the most advanced commercial satellites in the world in terms of adaptive beamforming for cost efficiencies, user performance improvements, and resilience to interference. They also set new commercial standards for solar power generation and thermal dissipation.

---

## 📊 Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | **Sputnik 1 (1957)** | **ViaSat-3 F3 (2026)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch Date** | October 4, 1957 | April 29, 2026 |
| **Country/Org** | Soviet Union | Viasat (USA) / SpaceX |
| **Launch Vehicle** | Modified R-7 ICBM | SpaceX Falcon Heavy |
| **Mass** | 83.6 kg | Thousands of kg (GEO-class) |
| **Orbit Type** | Low Earth Orbit (LEO) | Geostationary Orbit (GEO) |
| **Technology** | Radio transmitter, thermometer, fan | Ka-band, adaptive beamforming, electric propulsion |
| **Data/Capacity** | Beeping radio signal | **1+ Tbps** broadband throughput |
| **Purpose** | Prove orbital spaceflight was possible | Global broadband internet, aviation, maritime, defense |
| **Lifespan** | ~3 months | Designed for ~15+ years |
| **Impact** | Sparked the Space Race | Part of global multi-orbit network |

---

The contrast is extraordinary — from a simple beeping metal ball to a multi-terabit communications powerhouse, satellites have evolved beyond recognition in less than 70 years! 🌍
